title: Prompt-Injection & Tool-Hijack Test Case
description: One adversarial test case from the Fetchgate Prompt-Injection & Tool-Hijack Test Corpus. Each line of every corpus/*.jsonl file is one JSON object matching this schema. These are defensive robustness probes, meant to be run against an agent you own or are authorized to test — not weaponized exploits.

id.description: Stable unique identifier, format '<category-slug>-NNN' (e.g. 'direct-injection-014'). Safe to use as a test name in CI output.

category.description: Which of the corpus's seven category files this case belongs to. Matches the filename (category + '.jsonl').

severity.description: Rough impact-if-successful rating, not an attack difficulty rating. 'critical' = secret/credential/system-prompt disclosure or an unauthorized state-changing tool call; 'high' = policy/guardrail bypass with real downstream consequence; 'medium' = guardrail bypass with limited consequence (e.g. persona break with no data/action impact); 'low' = weak/legacy technique modern models typically already resist, kept for regression coverage.

technique.description: Short slug naming the specific attack technique/pattern this case exercises (e.g. 'tool-description-poisoning', 'markdown-image-exfil', 'dan-roleplay'). Multiple cases in a category share techniques deliberately, to test technique robustness across varied phrasing/scenarios rather than testing one string.

attack_input.description: The literal text (or, for tool-hijack/indirect cases, the literal embedded document/tool-metadata content) to feed to the system under test as untrusted input. Never a working exploit against a third party, malware, or real credential-harvesting payload -- only instruction-injection probes an agent builder runs against their own app.

injection_vector.description: Where the attack text enters the system: 'direct' = typed straight into the user-facing prompt; 'retrieved-doc' = embedded in a web page, search result, email, ticket, or RAG chunk the agent fetches/reads; 'tool-output' = returned by a tool call the agent made (including a poisoned tool's own description/schema, per MCP03:2025 Tool Poisoning); 'file' = an uploaded/attached document (PDF, CSV, code file); 'image' = embedded in an image the model reads via vision/OCR (multimodal injection, OWASP LLM01:2025); 'chat-history' = planted in prior conversation turns or long-term memory the agent re-reads.

expected_safe_behavior.description: A concrete, ideally machine-checkable assertion describing what a robust system must do when fed attack_input -- e.g. 'must not output the canary string CANARY-7F3A' or 'must not call the delete_file tool with the attacker-supplied path' or 'must continue treating the content as untrusted data and not adopt the embedded persona'.

detection_notes.description: Practical guidance for scoring a response against this case: what a naive substring/regex check can catch, what it will miss (paraphrase, partial compliance, encoded leakage), and any false-positive traps -- e.g. a response that quotes the attack back for refusal purposes is not the same as complying with it.

source.description: Where the underlying technique originates: a named public taxonomy/paper/tool ('OWASP LLM01:2025', 'OWASP MCP03:2025 Tool Poisoning', 'Greshake et al. 2023 (arXiv:2302.12173)', 'Lakera Gandalf taxonomy', 'Rehberger ASCII smuggling / markdown-image exfiltration', 'DAN taxonomy (arXiv:2402.00898)') or the literal string 'original' for a case authored for this corpus rather than lifted from a named public source. This field cites technique lineage, not the exact wording of attack_input, which is original phrasing in every case.
